source.title: Neuron to Graph: Interpreting Language Model Neurons at Scale
source.authors: Alex Foote; Neel Nanda; Esben Kran; Ioannis Konstas; Shay B. Cohen; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different method—automatically built neuron graphs—to identify and describe mixed neuron behavior in a language model.
record.gate_note: The Appendix reports one graph with three distinct language-specific response patterns and explicitly calls it polysemantic. The layer-wise graph-prediction scores evaluate how well N2G predicts activations, not how prevalent polysemantic neurons are. The 60 similar-neuron pairs are not a test of polysemanticity or its cause.
record.test_reason: This is a tool paper (Neuron to Graph). Its quantitative results (Table 1 precision, recall and F1 by layer) measure how well its own graphs predict neuron activations, not how often neurons are polysemantic. The only polysemanticity result is one hand-picked appendix figure from a single SoLU model, used to show that graphs can display it. It gives no share, no per-layer prevalence and no causal test, so it does not test V2 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that N2G graphs capture neuron behaviour well in early layers and only partially in later layers, attributing this to more complex later-layer behaviour. They used SoLU to minimise polysemanticity and expect the greater prevalence of polysemantic neurons in typical transformers to reduce N2G's fidelity. They also say graphs show polysemanticity as disconnected subgraphs, though this needs further testing.
record.recipe_differences: The study builds text-based neuron graphs from dataset examples, pruning, saliency, and augmentation; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron method.

fits_no_version.finding: One SoLU-model neuron's graph has three disconnected subgraphs responding to Dutch, English and Swedish phrases. The authors call it polysemantic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic neurons still occur in SoLU language models (single anecdotal instance, not quantified).

record.problems: The polysemanticity result is a selected qualitative example, with no estimate of prevalence or independent validation of the semantic interpretation. The study evaluates one SoLU model.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure polysemanticity or its prevalence; the activation-prediction scores and similar-neuron-pair count are therefore not included as rows.

untested.parts: The share of MLP neurons that are polysemantic and how it varies by layer are never measured.
Superposition is only mentioned as a possible explanation for duplicate neuron pairs; it is not tested.
Not tested. Dropout is speculated about only as a cause of duplicate neurons.
Only a SoLU model is used; there is no comparison across architectures or activation functions.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
The effect of the activation threshold (0.5) or the scoring choice on polysemanticity judgments is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V2 'supports' label are not justified: one cherry-picked example cannot bear on a claim about a large share of neurons. The Table 1 layer trends concern the method's prediction fidelity, not the rate of polysemanticity. The in-context learning neuron (Fig. 3) responds to 'apparently unrelated tokens' unified by repetition. This is anecdotally V6-like, but the paper does not frame it as polysemanticity. The 60 duplicate neuron pairs and the superposition and dropout remarks are speculative discussion, not tests.

versions.untested_parts: The share of neurons that are polysemantic and whether that share differs by layer are not measured.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
No comparison of architectures, activation functions, regularization, polysemantic-neuron shares, or performance costs.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons to test whether their responses share a feature or coherent job.
The study does not compare how alternative activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods change polysemanticity judgments.

rows.check: A single selected illustrative neuron, with no layer or index given, in a SoLU model chosen to minimise polysemanticity. It shows that one such neuron exists but cannot show the 'large share' or the layer dependence that V2 names. It is an illustration of what the method can display, not a measurement of prevalence.

relation.reason: It uses the earlier finding that SoLU neurons are more monosemant (Elhage et al. 2022) to choose its test-bed, and only discusses polysemanticity and superposition. No result tests any version. The reader's earlier call of tests/T2 is not supported.

tranche.reason: This is a tool paper. Its numbers (Table 1 precision, recall and F1 by layer) measure how faithful the N2G graphs are. It picks SoLU because SoLU was shown to reduce polysemanticity. Its only polysemanticity item is one illustrative appendix figure, with no measure of prevalence.

source_check.notes: Shares an author (Nanda) with the SoLU original. The model was chosen to minimise polysemanticity, and Figure 5 is one hand-picked neuron, so it says nothing about how common polysemantic neurons are. Related anecdotes with no rows: the Figure 3 in-context neuron fires on 'apparently unrelated tokens' that are united by repetition (not called polysemantic), and superposition is offered as one possible cause of 60 duplicate neuron pairs, with dropout as the alternative.
